Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0063", "row_sha256": "8feafabb151feb3a3b1bda15b74320f05935abe2f619096f3aefba3d9a28e963", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a prompt for a screen-reader audit of the North Harbor municipal permit portal. keep it to the application’s document-upload and application-review steps, not the whole site. people use those steps after they have filled in the permit form, and the audit is meant to show whether someone using a screen reader can understand what is happening and move through those parts without losing their place. the permit team has asked for a practical manual review, not a general accessibility statement. please make the request clear enough that someone else can follow it and report what they actually observe.

there is a staging build planned for this work, but i don't know whether it will be ready when the audit happens or whether its test accounts will be separated from production. only do the manual screen-reader audit if the staging build is available and the work can be done without opening, changing, or submitting production data. if either part of that condition is not true, don't try the live steps; instead review the audit notes that the permit team supplies and list the questions those notes leave unanswered. that is a different fallback task, not a smaller version of the live test. make the condition and the alternative explicit in the prompt so nobody treats staging availability alone as permission to proceed.

for the live path, use NVDA with Firefox on a desktop computer. stay with that setup rather than switching to a second screen reader or browser halfway through. use only the staging test account and the synthetic application and files prepared for the audit. the application is a fictional permit request for a small neighborhood street event. do not submit it or send anything to the permit team. the work is about the upload and review interaction; it isn't a review of the permit rules, the event's eligibility, or the wording of the whole form. if the staging account cannot get to those two steps using the prepared application, record that limitation instead of wandering into unrelated screens.

there are two points in the flow i want covered. first is the document-upload step: reach the upload control, identify its accessible name and any instructions attached to it, select one of the prepared sample files, and pay attention to the messages while the file is selected and processed. the sample set has one PDF and one JPG, both synthetic; use the PDF for the pass through the flow, and don't try to test file-size limits or unsupported formats. check how a person can tell that a file was added, whether its name is available to the screen reader, and whether there is a way to remove it before moving on. the second point is the application-review step immediately after upload. check how the screen reader moves through the summary, whether the entered information is understandable in its displayed order, and whether the person can identify the control for going back to make a correction. stop before any final submit action.

some of the details may look ordinary visually, so don't assume they are announced. the upload area has a short instruction, a file-picker control, a status message, and a list of selected files. one message in the current design reads “Attach a file to continue.” The audit should note whether that wording is announced at a useful time, but don't assume the wording itself is wrong just because it is short. When a file is selected, there may be a processing message before the file appears in the list; observe what NVDA says and whether focus stays somewhere understandable. The review page contains a heading, a compact summary of the event details, an uploaded-document entry, an edit link for returning to the form, and a continue control. The prompt should ask for observations about these things, not assert in advance that any of them fail.

please set out the live review in a practical order. 1) confirm the permitted setup and staging-only data boundary before interacting; 2) reach the upload step and inspect its control, instructions, file-selection feedback and removal option; 3) move to the review step and check the heading, summary, document entry, edit link and focus or reading order; 4) stop before final submission. Include keyboard navigation as part of the manual pass, since a screen-reader user still needs to move between controls, but don't turn this into a separate keyboard-only audit. Note the page or step and the action that led to any confusing announcement, missing name, unexpected focus change, or unclear route back. If something behaves as expected, record that too, so the notes are not only a list of defects.

for the fallback, the permit team will provide existing audit notes if the live condition isn't satisfied. read only those supplied notes and identify questions they leave open about the same upload and review steps. don't present those questions as observed failures and don't guess what NVDA or the portal would do. The notes may mention an older build, but don't assume it is the current staging build or use it for testing. if no notes are supplied, say in the table that the notes needed for the fallback were not provided; don't invent content to review. The fallback should still be useful to the permit team, but it should not become a request to schedule a test or to audit another part of the portal.

return only a table, with no introduction or closing paragraph. for a live pass, use columns for step or page, action, observed screen-reader or focus behavior, and any question or impact worth noting. For the notes-only fallback, use columns for the step or topic, what the supplied notes establish, and the question left open. Keep the report factual and concise, distinguish observations from questions, and include enough detail to locate each point in the flow. The result should not claim that the portal passed or failed as a whole. The permit team is deciding what to investigate after receiving the audit, and the review should leave that decision to them.", "output": "Create a practical prompt for a manual screen-reader audit of the North Harbor municipal permit portal. Limit the scope to the document-upload and application-review steps that follow completion of the permit form. The purpose is to determine whether a screen-reader user can understand what is happening and move through those steps without losing their place. This is not a general accessibility statement or a review of the entire site.

**Proceed only if the condition below is met:** the staging build is available, and the audit can be completed without opening, changing, or submitting production data. Staging availability alone is not sufficient. If either part of the condition is not met, do not attempt the live steps. Instead, review only the audit notes supplied by the permit team and list the questions those notes leave unanswered. Treat this as a distinct fallback task, not as a reduced live test.

### Live audit

Use NVDA with Firefox on a desktop computer throughout the manual pass. Use only the staging test account and the synthetic application and files prepared for the audit. The application is a fictional permit request for a small neighborhood street event. Do not submit it or send anything to the permit team. Do not assess permit rules, the event’s eligibility, or the wording of the entire form. If the staging account cannot reach the two steps using the prepared application, record that limitation and do not explore unrelated screens.

Follow this order:

1. Confirm that the permitted setup is available and that the staging-only data boundary is satisfied before interacting.
2. At the document-upload step, reach the upload control and identify its accessible name and any instructions attached to it. Select the prepared PDF for the pass through the flow. The sample set also includes a synthetic JPG, but do not test file-size limits or unsupported formats. Observe the feedback while the file is selected and processed, whether the file name is available to the screen reader, how the user can tell the file was added, and whether there is a way to remove it before continuing.
3. Move to the application-review step immediately after upload. Check how the screen reader moves through the summary, whether the entered information is understandable in its displayed order, and whether the user can identify the control for returning to make a correction. The review page contains a heading, a compact summary of the event details, an uploaded-document entry, an edit link, and a continue control. Observe these elements without assuming in advance that any one of them fails.
4. Stop before any final submit action.

Include keyboard navigation as part of the manual screen-reader pass, since the user still needs to move between controls. Do not turn it into a separate keyboard-only audit. Note the page or step and the action leading to any confusing announcement, missing name, unexpected focus change, or unclear route back. Record behavior that works as expected as well as behavior that raises a question, so the report is not limited to defects.

The upload area includes a short instruction, a file-picker control, a status message, and a list of selected files. One message in the current design reads, “Attach a file to continue.” Note whether this wording is announced at a useful time; do not assume it is wrong merely because it is short. A processing message may appear before the selected file appears in the list. Record what NVDA says and whether focus remains somewhere understandable.

### Notes-only fallback

If the live-audit condition is not met, read only the existing audit notes supplied by the permit team. Identify questions they leave open about the same upload and review steps. Do not describe those questions as observed failures or guess what NVDA or the portal would do. Notes may refer to an older build; do not assume that build is the current staging build or test it. If no notes are supplied, state in the table that the notes needed for the fallback were not provided. Do not invent material to review, request a test to be scheduled, or expand the scope to another part of the portal.

Return only a table, with no introduction or closing paragraph. For a live pass, use columns for step or page, action, observed screen-reader or focus behavior, and any question or impact worth noting. For the fallback, use columns for step or topic, what the supplied notes establish, and the question left open. Keep the report factual and concise, distinguish observations from questions, and include enough detail to locate each point in the flow. Do not claim that the portal passed or failed as a whole; leave the permit team to decide what to investigate after receiving the audit."}]
